content.content:
c14e24a5eedb7a6aed70caaa36c9e2a69c75c9d1
fleet-baseline: follow every member to current, report outcomes not dispatches (#1294)

A dispatch POST returning 204 says a run was QUEUED and nothing more.
Reporting those 204s reports the sweep's own outgoing calls rather than the
fleet, and reads as fleet-wide delivery when it was not: a run announced
`13 fired, 0 failed` while 9 of the 13 took nothing (#1292).

So the lever now follows each dispatched member to a terminal condition read
off the member itself — does its own settings file stamp the engine and every
declared pack at the versions canon publishes? — and reports per member:

  converged          was behind canon, reached its versions during this run
  already-current    was at canon's versions before the dispatch
  did-not-converge   its scheduler ran and it is still behind
  never-started      the dispatch was accepted and no run followed it
  unknown            the member could not be read

`already-current` is a success in its own right. Such a member's update
correctly declines and it does no work; folding that into a failure would
report a fault where there is none, and into `converged` would claim work
that did not happen.

The headline count becomes `current of dispatched`, and the run FAILS when a
dispatched member never got there — the case the old report showed as a win.

The version comparison is not new code: `canonVersions` and
`classifyFreshness` already exist in this pack for the roster's drift issues
and are imported rather than reimplemented.

This reverses #649's "give up the follow", on the owner's call (#1293). What
that retired was a blind fixed wait every run paid whatever the fleet was
doing, which forced the lever to be a standalone workflow. follow-to-current
polls a real terminal condition and each member leaves the loop the moment it
reads current, so an already-current fleet finishes on the first pass in
seconds and the lever stays an ordinary queue task. `code_work_timeout` rises
to 1800s so the 20-minute follow budget finishes well inside it — a run the
platform kills never prints the report it spent the time earning.

Stated in the report itself: "current" is a claim about PUBLISHED VERSION
NUMBERS, so canon content shipped without a version bump is invisible to it.
That is exactly the #1292 case, and the word must not imply more than was
checked.

The retired decision is purged where it was written down — the pack RULES.md,
both READMEs, and the task test that asserted the worker "never follows".

Refs #1293

Co-authored-by: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
===EEC43A5===
eec43a537770f4f3d2ecc76a64bb52added75f53
Make the scheduler and executor workflows thin wrappers over engine code (#1290)

`.github/workflows/` is the one vendored path a converge cannot push into:
a member's copy of these two files moves only through a PR a human merges,
in every repo, while every engine module converges nightly. So logic or
prose left in the YAML costs a fleet-wide human-merged PR to change.

Move the three inline `github-script` programs into engine modules the
workflows now name in a single-line `run:`:

  queue/drain-dispatch.mjs        the post-scheduler-run drain's dispatch
  queue/workflow-failure.mjs      the one-open-issue failure escalation
  queue/executor-continuation.mjs the dead-run chain and its cap

All three reuse the engine helpers the YAML was re-implementing
(`dispatchWorkflow`, `createIssue`, `ensureLabels`), which is also how the
dispatch and the create stop being judged by their response bodies.
`dispatchWorkflow` gains an optional `inputs` argument for the chain depth.

The prose moves to those modules' headers; the YAML keeps only the comments
a reader of the YAML alone needs — the literal label spellings the event
trigger cannot decode, the stale-copy note on the drain gate, and the
`# claudinite:secrets` marker the converge stamps against.

Guards, since a thin wrapper names its logic by literal path:
- `scheduler-workflows-are-thin` (blocking, world) refuses `github-script`
  and a block `run:` in either stub and either canon copy;
- a vendor-set test asserts every module the stubs name is actually shipped,
  the failure that would otherwise be a queue that silently stops draining;
- a `thin-workflows` rehearsal shape — `old-workflows` from the other end.

The scheduler workflow's header named a `scheduler-stub-parity` check that
exists nowhere in the tree; the real guard is the pair of drift tests in
engine-tests/scheduler/converge-wiring.test.mjs, now named instead.

Refs #1289

Co-authored-by: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
===C0DD572===
c0dd57214920e66b4aa3cb9c0e6a6d04c1f2e089
Gate wiki-growth on pending product-wiki paths, not a label (#1257)

The `product-wiki-growth` label existed for one reader: the wiki-growth
precondition, declining while a previous round's PR sat unreviewed. Every
growth PR carried a marker nothing else looked at, and a PR opened without
it was silently stacked on.

The `prs` collector now resolves each open PR's changed paths, and the
precondition declines on a pending `product-wiki/` change in any open PR —
a human's edit in flight as much as the task's own. Paths that could not be
read are `null`, a third state the gate declines on rather than reading as
clear, which is also what carries it through an engine older than this one.

`prs.open[].labels` goes with the label: it was there for this gate alone.

Closes #1256

Co-authored-by: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
===BD77C1F===
bd77c1fcc595d903876b8bcb2b59adb75d1b398e
Keep the dashboard's import graph free of node: builtins (#1287)

The page is served as raw ESM, so every relative import it reaches is
fetched by the browser. settings-read.mjs reached engine/settings-file.mjs,
which imports node:fs and node:path for its disk probe, and the page failed
its first module load with nothing rendered.

The settings-file names move into their own browser-pure module, re-exported
from settings-file.mjs so no disk-side caller changes.

The pin that was meant to catch this walked a hand-kept list of engine
modules and never gained this one. It now walks the page's real import graph
from the entry point index.html names.

Closes #1286

Co-authored-by: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>

{"number":1301,"title":"Stop stamping secrets by name into the executor workflow — pass the whole secrets context once","body":"Sub-issue of #1296, addressing its stamping half.

## The problem

`.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml` names every secret it passes, and the wiring converge regenerates that list from `required_secrets` plus configured endpoint tokens (`converge-wiring.mjs:106-117`). That makes the file's content a function of the task set — and it is the one file a converge **cannot write**, because Actions refuses the `GITHUB_TOKEN` under `.github/workflows/` and the refusal rejects the whole ref.

So every new secret or endpoint token needs a human-merged PR in every member. #1296 is what that costs: `hitbut` had `CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN` set the whole time, but its live executor workflow predated the stamping, the agent could not start, and the only lane that delivers a staged workflow is the agentic apply stage the agent was needed for. Permanently wedged.

## The change

Actions has exactly one way to pass all of them: `${{ toJSON(secrets) }}`, which expands the whole `secrets` context into one variable. (`secrets: inherit` does not help — it is reusable-workflow-call only, and the callee still names each one.)

The executor step carries one static line:

```yaml
CLAUDINITE_SECRETS: ${{ toJSON(secrets) }}
```

and the workflow stops being a function of the task set. Nothing about secrets can wedge a member's workflow delivery again.

The executor then parses that bag and, per task, hands code-work **only the names that task declared**. That is a tightening, not a loosening: today `code-work-run.mjs:67` spreads the executor's whole `process.env` into the child, so all three stamped secrets reach the work step of every code-work task though only 6 of ~22 declare one — contradicting `docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md:1286` ("whose env carries exactly the declared names"). Parsing a bag is what makes that line true.

`invoke.mjs` reads its endpoint token from the same bag, and its error message can finally distinguish the two causes #1296 says it conflates.

## Compatibility

Fielded members keep an old executor workflow that stamps names directly and sets no `CLAUDINITE_SECRETS`, and that file moves only by human-merged PR — so the reader accepts both: the bag when present, `process.env[NAME]` when it is not. Retirement is gated on no member still running a stamping executor workflow, never a date.

## Known cost

Every repo secret reaches the executor **job**'s env (not any task subprocess, which is filtered). And masking is registered per exact literal, so a secret containing `"`, `\` or a newline appears JSON-escaped in the bag and would not be masked if something printed it — theoretical for token-shaped values, but real. Recorded here rather than discovered later.

{"number":1174,"title":"fleet-baseline can only force `update` — there is no lever for any other task fleet-wide","body":"`fleet-baseline` is the fleet's only forcing lever, and it hard-codes what it forces:

```js
// packs/claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/tasks/fleet-baseline/force-fleet-baseline.mjs
export const FORCED_TASK = 'update';
```

Everything underneath it is already generic — `fireScheduler(gh, fullName, ref, taskId)` takes the id as an argument, and the member-side `planWake` accepts a whitespace/comma-separated list of `task` or `pack/task` ids and *creates* the standing item when one is missing. Only the constant is fixed.

So "force task X across the fleet" has exactly one route today: dispatch each member's `claudinite-scheduler.yml` yourself with `wake: X`. That needs Actions-write on every member, which is the credential `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` exists to hold and which an interactive session scoped to a handful of repos does not have. The alternative — attaching every member to the session — is per-repo manual work, which reliably does not happen.

Surfaced doing #1158's "force `usage-fold` fleet-wide" step. It cost nothing there: the converge `fleet-baseline` forces lands a commit on each member's default branch, and that commit is exactly what `usage-fold`'s movement precondition gates on, so forcing `update` forced the fold one hop later by accident. The next task that wants a fleet-wide force will not be so lucky.

**Shape of the fix** (the lever's `README` already documents the parameter-bag pattern this would join): a `WAKE` context parameter beside the existing `REPOS` / `DRY_RUN` / `INCLUDE_DORMANT`, defaulting to `update` so every existing item keeps its meaning, passed through to `fireScheduler` and named in the run summary. The summary line already reads *"Asked each covered member's own `claudinite-scheduler.yml` to wake its `update` item"* — it would just stop being a constant.

Two things to get right, both learned the hard way in this repo:

- **The protocol spans repos.** The dispatch input is read by each member's own vendored scheduler stub, so a new spelling has to be one every fielded stub already understands. `wake` itself is unchanged here — only which id travels in it — so this should be safe, but it is the class of change that broke Shepherd's only caller in #929.
- **A parameter that stops being read must fail loudly** (#974). If `WAKE` is added, an item naming a task no declared pack owns must land in the summary's `failed` list, not dispatch `update` silently because the name did not resolve.

Not urgent — nothing is blocked on it — but it is a hole in the fleet's control surface that is invisible until someone needs it.","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1174","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","labels":["quick-win"],"assignees":[],"comments":1,"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-08-21T15:19:37Z","updated_at":"2026-08-23T18:00:17Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":false,"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}

{"number":1237,"title":"Chain 3/3: retire the twice-daily-cron migration tolerances","body":"Link 3 of #1225's execution chain — the last one, and the **delayed task that merges #1234**. Everything you need is here.

```
Blocked-by: #1236
Retry-every: 7 days
Model: sonnet
```

## What this removes

#1234 is written, reviewed, rebased onto `main` and mergeable. It empties `LEGACY_FREQUENCIES`, so `hourly` / `daily-2h` / `daily-1h` / `daily+1h` stop being accepted in a task declaration, and it stops `scheduler-workflow-shape` accepting the legacy hourly cron.

**It must not be merged early, and the reason is measurable.** `scheduler-workflow-shape` is severity `blocking`; on #1234's branch it emits a finding for an hourly cron; and a member's converge **withholds** `.github/workflows/` — the one path it cannot push — so a member holding the old cron cannot fix itself. Merging before every member's workflow PR has landed turns the whole fleet red on a file none of them can repair.

## What makes this step's world ready

#1236 closed, **and** the precondition below reads true. Converge-confirmable, never a date — if it does not hold yet, this is a wait, not a failure.

**No member's own task declarations still name a retired frequency.** Canon packs are already migrated; what matters is each member's `.claudinite/local/packs/*/tasks/*/task.mjs`, which is member-authored and which no vendoring pass rewrites. Grep each member for `frequency: 'hourly'`, `'daily-2h'`, `'daily-1h'`, `'daily+1h'`.

Retiring early does not merely fail such a task. `periodMs` also feeds the janitor's stale-ready bound and the precondition's signal window, so an un-normalized token makes a daily task judged against a bound it was never sized for — a `needs-human` park on every sweep.

## The playbook

1. Check the precondition across every member. If any still declares a retired token: comment which member and which file on #1225, push `Not-before` forward by `Retry-every`, clear this issue's `task:status:*` label, and leave it open. No other comment — the bumped field is the record. Fixing that member's declaration is the way to unblock this, and is worth doing.
2. Precondition holds → fetch #1234's branch and confirm it is still current against `main`; rebase if `main` has moved under it.
3. Run the full suite: `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`, and `check_the_work`.
4. Green → merge #1234 (squash).

**Already done, 2026-08-22 — do not redo:** the branch was rebased onto `main` after #1230 merged, and the `pack-version-bumped` false green called out in #1234's body is resolved — `claudinite-lifecycle` is `60822.3` against main's `60822.2`, and `check_the_work` is clean against the true base. Step 2 is a re-check, not the original rebase.

Note the two tolerances have **different** gates. The cron half's gate — every member's workflow PR landed — is satisfied by #1235. If the frequency half is still blocked long after, split the commit and merge the cron half alone.

## What counts as this step having worked

#1234 merged, suite green, and no member red on its next converge.

## How it ends

Comment on #1225 that the tolerances are retired and the migration is complete, then close this issue as completed. #1225 can close with it.

{"number":1236,"title":"Chain 2/3: verify the twice-daily cron in production — 2 scheduler runs a day, not 24","body":"Link 2 of #1225's execution chain. Everything you need is here.

```
Blocked-by: #1235
Not-before: 2026-08-25T06:00:00Z
Retry-every: 1 day
Model: sonnet
```

## What this proves

The whole point of the change: the scheduler was **71% of private Actions spend** at ~26 min/day per member, because Actions bills each job rounded up and the cron fired 24 times a day to do about 13 minutes of work. Two ticks a day should make that ~2 min/day. Nothing so far has measured a real repo — only the simulator.

## What makes this step's world ready

#1235 closed (every member on the new cron), **and** at least one full UTC day has elapsed since, so there is a complete day to count.

## What to observe

For each **private** member — the ones that cost anything; public repos are free and unlimited:

1. **The count.** Scheduler workflow runs for one complete UTC day. Expect exactly **2**. Baseline: 24.
2. **Nothing was dropped.** No task's standing item is missing its occurrence for that day — a cheaper cron that quietly stopped instantiating work is a regression, not a saving.
3. **The risk the simulator could not model.** A whole day's chain now settles serially inside one executor run. Read the longest executor run's duration against the workflow's `timeout-minutes: 350`. The simulator's task durations are fixtures, so this is the first real read of whether a member's day actually fits.

## What counts as this step having worked

Every private member shows 2 scheduler runs for the measured day, no missing occurrences, and no executor run near its timeout.

## When the check fails

Comment what you read and **leave this issue open** — closing releases the next link.

- Still 24 runs on some member → its workflow never landed; reopen #1235's question there rather than proceeding.
- Missing occurrences → this is a real regression in the cadence change. Reopen #1225 with what is missing and stop the chain.
- An executor run near the timeout → do **not** fail the step, but say so plainly on #1225: it is the residual risk the plan named, and it wants its own issue rather than silence.

## How it ends

Comment the per-member figures on #1225 — runs/day before and after, and the longest executor run — then close this issue as completed. That close releases Link 3.

{"number":1224,"title":"Eliminate avoidable GitHub-platform assumptions from packs","body":"A census of GitHub-platform assumptions (the platform, not plain git) across the engine and every pack found 367 distinct assumptions counted once per component — 81 in the engine, 286 across the packs.

Scoping this work to the packs, and excluding `git-github` (which owns GitHub as a subject, 38 assumptions), leaves ~248 in scope. Of those, roughly 40–50 are avoidable and fall in two buckets:

**Bucket 1 — not actually GitHub assumptions (~13).** Generic-CI facts phrased in GitHub vocabulary, which the census counts only because the wording names a GitHub feature. They hold on any CI system:

- `firebase` (4) — "release-workflow variables", "workflow dispatch"
- `web-scraping` (3) — runner IP blocks, "repository secrets", commit-step durability
- `macos` (2) — secret-gated signing lane, build annotations
- `spec-driven-product` (2) — CI-gated merge, automated release cut
- `aws-sam` (1) — deploy-workflow staleness caveat
- `research-project` (1) — branch/commit/PR conventions

The fix is a phrasing pass to platform-neutral wording. No behavior changes.

**Bucket 2 — restatements of facts another pack or skill owns (~25–30).** These violate the corpus's own dependency rule ("say what A needs from B; don't re-spell how B does its job"). Repeat offenders:

- "`GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot write `.github/workflows/`" — re-explained in `claudinite-dashboard`, `claudinite-fleet-sheepdog`, `claudinite-lifecycle` when the engine's withhold lane owns it
- "`GITHUB_TOKEN` pushes fire no workflows" — re-derived in `claudinite-dashboard`, `chrome-extension`, `static-website` when `git-github` owns it
- the exact-title-tracker / issue-creation-lands-open / no-comment-update-tool cluster — owned by the `unattended-agents` skill, restated in `tidy-repo`, `jwt`, `product-wiki`
- squash-merge evidence rules — owned by `git-github`, restated in `basics` and `tidy-repo` skills

Two exemptions constrain this bucket: vendored workflow stubs must stay self-contained (their comments travel into member repos, where a canon reference dangles), and `task.md` files are read standalone by executor sessions, so some restatement there is deliberate context rather than drift.

**Out of scope.** The remaining ~200 are inherent — the dashboard's rate-limit/OAuth/Pages model, sheepdog's fleet API vocabulary, lifecycle's PR delivery, growth's issue-queue semantics, the two vendored release pipelines, basics' issue→PR lifecycle, tidy-repo's triage primitives. Eliminating those means dropping the capability or building a forge-abstraction seam, neither of which is justified without a second consumer. The per-pack REST-client duplication is likewise deliberate (#959).

**Done when** both buckets are landed and a re-run of the per-component census shows the reduction.","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1224","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","labels":["needs-decision"],"assignees":[],"comments":2,"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-08-22T11:21:03Z","updated_at":"2026-08-23T17:59:53Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":false,"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}

{"number":1240,"title":"Remove the tidy-branches task from tidy-repo","body":"Drop `tidy-branches` from the `tidy-repo` pack. The pack keeps its other two dimensions, `tidy-issues` and `tidy-prs`; only the branch sweep goes.

## The change

Delete `packs/tidy-repo/tasks/tidy-branches/` (both `task.mjs` and `task.md`) and sweep every reference to it. Known referencing files:

- `packs/tidy-repo/pack.mjs` — the task roster
- `packs/tidy-repo/pack.test.mjs` — assertions naming the task
- `packs/tidy-repo/README.md`
- `packs/tidy-repo/RULES.md` — names the three tasks and the "branches — assess only" half of the policy
- `packs/tidy-repo/tasks/tidy-issues/task.md` — mentions it
- `packs/tidy-repo/skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md` — its worker skill

Decide as part of the work whether `single-branch-status` goes with it: with no task invoking it, it is a skill nothing calls. Removing it is the default; keep it only if something outside `tidy-branches` still reaches it, and say which in the PR.

`RULES.md` currently states the policy over three dimensions and specifically covers branches ("assess only; never delete, push, merge, or close"). With the task gone, that prose has no runner — rewrite the policy to the two dimensions that remain rather than leaving branch rules stranded.

Do not edit `.claudinite/local/usage.GENERATED.json`; it is generated and holds historical counts.

## Done looks like

- No `tidy-branches` anywhere outside generated files and historical records (`git grep tidy-branches` clean).
- `packs/tidy-repo` pack version bumped (the `pack-version-bumped` check requires it for any pack change).
- Full suite green: `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`.
- The task's standing tracker issue, if one is open in this repo, gets a closing comment saying the task was removed — the sweep will never rewrite it again.

Model: opus
Automerge: if-narrow

```
node /scheduler/queue/converge-item.mjs --issue  --outcome ... --summary ...
```

directly as a subprocess. That script (via `engine/scheduler/signals/gh.mjs`'s `makeGh`) talks to `api.github.com` straight over `fetch`, authorized with `process.env.GITHUB_TOKEN` — the Action-side credential, per the DESIGN comment atop `gh.mjs`: "engine/scheduler/ is the one place that legitimately uses the Action's GITHUB_TOKEN — everything session-side stays MCP-only."

But `queue/instructions.md` step 6 *is* session-side — it is the procedure every agent session follows to converge the one work item it was fired for (a Claude Code session, not an Actions job). This session's own system prompt states plainly it has no `gh` CLI and no direct GitHub API access, and must use the GitHub MCP server tools for all GitHub interactions. Confirmed live on this run (#1097):

- `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` is unset by default in this session (`converge-item: GITHUB_REPOSITORY is not set`).
- Setting it and calling the script directly returns a 403 straight from the GitHub REST API: `{"message":"GitHub access is not enabled for this session. An org admin must connect the Claude GitHub App for this organization."}` — a policy boundary, not a fixable env-var wrinkle.

This is the same class of break as #1133: a script written for the Actions-job execution context (`gh.mjs`'s `makeGh`) silently fails once the same work runs inside an MCP-only agent session — except here the break isn't silent, it's a hard stop on the one step every work item's session-side execution must perform: convergence. As written, no work item picked up by an agent session (`queue/instructions.md`'s normal path) can converge in code — it either gets hand-converged (which `instructions.md` explicitly says not to do) or sits stuck wearing `task:agent` until the janitor's 3h agent-leash reclaims it as dead.

The repo already has the right shape for this split: `deliver-pr.md` (AGENT lane, MCP-backed) beside `land-pr.mjs` (CODE lane, Action-side `gh.mjs`) for PR delivery. `converge-item.mjs` needs the same — an MCP-backed convergence path `queue/instructions.md` can actually invoke from a session, mirroring what `convergeItem()` already does (comment, swap labels, close/park, release dependents, request write-back) but over `mcp__github__*` tools instead of `gh.mjs`.

Observed on #1097 (`Request: #1095`): the actual requested work completed and was verified successfully — #1095 was checked and closed with the evidence. Only this item's own code-side convergence failed, for the reason above. {"number":1296,"title":"Withheld-workflow deadlock: a member whose endpoint token is not yet stamped can never deliver the workflow that would stamp it","body":"Confirmed on `missingbulb/hitbut` (missingbulb/hitbut#102), stuck since 2026-08-21.

## The loop

1. The agent session is started by `engine/scheduler/queue/invoke.mjs`, which reads the endpoint token out of **the executor job's env** (`env[endpoint.tokenEnv]`).
2. That variable reaches the job only from `.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml`, stamped below the `# claudinite:secrets` marker by the wiring converge.
3. The converge **cannot write** `.github/workflows/` — the Actions `GITHUB_TOKEN` is refused there, and the refusal rejects the whole ref — so `updates/pack-update.mjs` withholds the file into `.claudinite/pending-workflows/`.
4. The **only** thing that delivers a staged workflow is the agentic apply stage, `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/tasks/update/task.md`. Nothing in `engine/` or `updates/` moves it — I grepped every consumer of `PENDING_DIR`.
5. The agent cannot start, because of (1).

So a member that reaches step 3 with an **unstamped** token can never reach step 4. It is not slow, it is not retrying — it is permanently wedged, and no converge, no wake, no force, and no `fleet-baseline` can move it. Only a credential that may write `.github/workflows/` — a human push or a human-merged PR — breaks it.

## Who is exposed

Any member whose live `claudinite-executor.yml` predates the stamping of an invocation endpoint token it now needs. That is not a one-off: it is the ordinary state of every member between "the endpoint gets configured" and "the next apply stage delivers the workflow" — and the deadlock is precisely that the second never happens if the first is what the agent needed.

On `hitbut` the correct file has been sitting in `.claudinite/pending-workflows/` with the right line in it the whole time.

## It is also undiagnosable as written

`invoke.mjs:105-110` observes an empty env var and reports:

> the Actions secret `CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN` for invocation endpoint "default" is not set in this repo

That asserts a cause the code cannot see. The secret was set the whole time; the workflow simply never passed it. I read the message, believed it, and filed the wrong fix — the owner caught it. Anyone reading that message goes to the Secrets page, sees the secret present, and has nowhere to go next.

The message should say what was observed and name both causes, e.g.:

> `CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN` is empty in this job. Either the repository secret is not set, **or** `.github/workflows/claudinite-executor.yml` does not pass it — check for an undelivered `.claudinite/pending-workflows/claudinite-executor.yml`, which is the usual cause.

## Worth deciding

- **Break the loop in code.** The staged→live move is a file rename with no judgment in it; the reason it is agentic is the *credential*, not the decision. Is there a lane that can deliver it without an agent — the maintenance PR itself carrying the move, for a human to merge, so the deadlock degrades to "waiting on a human" instead of "wedged forever"?
- **Detect it.** A member with a non-empty `.claudinite/pending-workflows/` that has not shrunk in N days is a wedged member by definition. `fleet-roster` already reads member trees; this is one existence check away and would have caught `hitbut` on day one.
- **Fix the message** at `invoke.mjs:110` regardless — it is cheap and it is what cost the diagnosis.

I have not picked one; the first is a real design question and the second is a policy call.","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1296","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","assignees":[],"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-08-23T16:04:00Z","updated_at":"2026-08-23T16:04:00Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":true,"sub_issues_summary":{"total":1,"completed":0,"percent_completed":0},"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}

{"number":1295,"title":"A member whose Actions jobs cannot start has no escalation path — report-failure dies with everything else","body":"Found while diagnosing why `missingbulb/missingbulbwebsite` had not converged since 2026-08-21 (missingbulb/MissingBulbWebsite#217).

## The gap

`claudinite-scheduler.yml`'s `report-failure` job exists so that a scheduled run going red reaches a human — a scheduled run reaches no one otherwise. But it is an ordinary job on an ordinary runner, `needs: [scheduler-run, drain]`, in the same repository as the thing that failed.

So when the failure mode is **"this repo cannot start Actions jobs at all"** — a spending limit, Actions disabled, a runner the repo cannot get — `report-failure` fails for exactly the same reason, in the same ~3 seconds, and files nothing. The louder the breakage, the quieter the escalation.

Observed on `missingbulbwebsite`: ~30 consecutive hourly runs, `scheduler-run` failure + `report-failure` failure + `drain` skipped, no steps, no logs, no issue filed, for over two days. The mount froze on 2026-08-21 and nothing in that repo said a word.

This is not hypothetical elsewhere either — it is the general shape of any escalation that depends on the resource it is reporting the loss of.

## What did notice

Only the fleet enforcer, from **outside** the repo: `fleet-roster`'s drift issue (missingbulb/Shepherd#95), open since 2026-08-20. That is the right instinct — self-maintenance cannot detect its own absence — but a drift issue is a standing report nobody is paged by, and it sat for three days.

Since #1294, `fleet-baseline` now **fails its run** when a dispatched member does not reach canon's versions, which gives that observation teeth for the first time. This issue is about whether the member-side half should stop pretending it can self-report.

## Worth deciding

- Should `report-failure` be dropped from the stub as **structurally unable** to cover the worst failure mode, leaving fleet-side detection (`fleet-roster` + `fleet-baseline`) as the honest single owner of "this member is broken"? It would also thin the workflow further, which #1289 wanted.
- Or should it stay for the failure modes it *can* report (a task that threw, a bad token) while the fleet owns the rest — in which case its own README/comment should say plainly what it cannot catch, so nobody reads a quiet Actions tab as health.
- Either way: should `fleet-roster` escalate a member that has been behind for **N days** differently from one behind by a version — a standing drift issue is clearly not enough signal on its own?

I have not picked one; the first two are a real trade and the third is a policy call.","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1295","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","assignees":[],"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-08-23T15:43:27Z","updated_at":"2026-08-23T15:43:27Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":false,"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}

{"number":1291,"title":"Verify in production: the drain job actually runs drain-dispatch.mjs","body":"#1290 moved the scheduler workflow's drain from an inline `github-script` block to `node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/drain-dispatch.mjs`. Unit tests cover the module, and the thin workflow itself has been watched running green on `missingbulb/Shepherd` ([run 32638669087](https://github.com/missingbulb/Shepherd/actions/runs/32638669087)) — but on that run the queue was empty, so the `drain` job was **skipped by its own gate** and the new module has never actually executed inside a member's Actions job.

That is the one path worth proving live. It runs on every tick that leaves work pickable, and its failure mode is silent: the workflow parses, the run goes green, node exits on a bad path or a refused dispatch, and the queue simply stops draining. No test can answer whether the vendored path resolves and the job's token can fire the dispatch from inside a member repo — only a real run can.

(The two sibling modules, `workflow-failure.mjs` and `executor-continuation.mjs`, fire only when a run fails or dies. They cannot be forced without breaking something, and their unit coverage is the mechanism that comes back for them.)

Original-issue: #1289
In-production-when: `missingbulb/Shepherd` has a `claudinite-scheduler.yml` run created after 2026-08-23T12:11Z whose `drain` job has a conclusion of `success` (not `skipped`) — read the run's jobs, not the run's own conclusion, since the run is green either way.
Verify: that drain job's log shows the line `- dispatched the executor on  to drain whatever this scheduler run created`, and a `claudinite-executor.yml` run of event `workflow_dispatch` exists in Shepherd within a few minutes after it. Pass = both. Fail = the drain job errored, or it succeeded with no matching executor run.
Not-before: 2026-08-24T06:00:00Z
Retry-every: 1 day

Model: sonnet

---

### For the run

1. Read `In-production-when:` against Shepherd's real workflow runs. Never infer it from a merge, a green run, or elapsed time — a scheduler run whose `drain` job is `skipped` does **not** satisfy it; keep waiting.
2. **Live** → run `Verify:`. Passes: comment the run URL, the drain job's log line and the matching executor run URL, then close this issue as completed. Fails: reopen #1289 with a comment saying what was asserted, what happened instead and where you read it; comment here linking that; close this issue as completed.
3. **Not yet live** → push `Not-before:` forward by 1 day, clear this issue's `task:status:*` label, and leave it open. #1287 removed the `node:fs`/`node:path` import that reached the dashboard's browser module graph through `engine/settings-file.mjs`, which was leaving the published page a blank screen (#1286). The page loads clean from a local checkout, and the new `browser-graph.test.mjs` pins the property in CI — but neither watches the **published** site.

Production here is another repo: the dashboard is served from GitHub Pages by the member that declares `claudinite-dashboard` (`https://missingbulb.github.io//`, Shepherd at the time of filing). The canon's bytes reach it only after that member's nightly converge re-vendors `engine/` and the pack, and after its own Pages workflow deploys. Neither had happened when this was filed, and neither can be forced from the canon.

One thing to watch while verifying: a converge push is authored with the default `GITHUB_TOKEN`, which fires no `on: push` workflow (#1094). A converged mount with a stale deployed site is a real possible outcome, and it is a failure to report, not a wait to extend.

Original-issue: #1286
In-production-when: the deployed dashboard's own `packs/claudinite-dashboard/settings-read.mjs` — fetched from the live Pages URL, not from any repo — imports `../../engine/settings-file-names.mjs`, and `engine/settings-file-names.mjs` is fetchable beside it at the same site.

Pass = no fetched module imports a `node:` specifier, `engine/settings-file.mjs` is either absent from the graph or no longer reached by `settings-read.mjs`, and the page's own HTML/script fetches return 200. {"number":1284,"title":"Add cloudflare-workers pack","body":"### Comment class: other

Weekly `canon-curation/growth-discover-packs` fleet sweep (#1279), Context-scoped to 16 members.

## The gap

`missingbulb/hitbut` is the fleet's first Cloudflare Workers backend — a single Worker bound to
D1, R2, Vectorize and Queues, deployed and tested with Wrangler (`src/backend/`,
`dev/requirements/server/`, `dev/tools/preflight.ts`/`smoke.ts`). No canon pack homes Cloudflare
Workers, and the repo demonstrates real, portable gotchas with no false-positive-free static
signature — deploy-vs-migration ordering, a hand-declared `env.ts` avoiding a Workers-types/DOM
collision once a frontend shares the repo, testing against real `workerd` from the committed
`wrangler.toml`, seeding D1 from the shipped migration files, why local Wrangler emulation can't
prove Cloudflare's own D1/R2/Queues, and parsing a Wrangler preflight's own error markers to tell
*missing* from *unknown*.

Single-member evidence, but per the worthiness bar this is the weaker-but-qualifying case: the
knowledge is plainly general (any future Cloudflare Workers project would want every rule here),
not this product's non-transferable particulars. Stripped of hitbut's product vocabulary
(persona/utterance/finding/corpus never appear).

## What's in this PR

- `packs/cloudflare-workers/` — `RULES.md` (7 rules), `pack.mjs` (fingerprint: a
  `wrangler.toml`/`.jsonc`/`.json` at the repo root or one directory down), `README.md`
  (rule index + provenance), `badge.svg`.
- `packs/README.md` — index row.
- `packs/directory.GENERATED.md` — regenerated (`node --test engine-tests/pack-directory.test.mjs`).

## Verification

- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 2663 pass, 0 fail (the one pre-existing shallow-clone
  failure on `main` also cleared on this checkout).
- `node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs` — 0 blocking, exit 0; no findings on the new pack.

## Follow-ups (tracker only, not this PR)

- `missingbulb/LaughCounter` and `missingbulb/WIP` already carry the fingerprint for the existing
  `macos` and `flutter` packs respectively but haven't declared them; `missingbulb/TLDR` likewise
  for `aws-sam`. Left for the fingerprint sweep (`fleet-add-missing-packs`), per the task's own
  rule that a homed technology gets a "should declare" tracker note, never a new pack or an issue
  from this run.
- `missingbulb/EdFringeAllocator` calls the Anthropic API directly for its LLM scheduler, but the
  evidence is one thin script with no recurring gotcha beyond ordinary API-calling practice —
  considered and rejected as too shallow for a pack.

Logged to #642 (`Claudinite tracker: Discover Canon Packs`).

{"number":1285,"title":"prose-to-checks-sweep: two conversions (doc-pointer-resolves, shared-tree-immutable)","body":"## Summary

Weekly prose-to-checks sweep over `.claudinite/local/packs` and `packs` (per the [prose-to-checks](packs/claudinite-growth/skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md) skill). Surveyed all 34 canon packs plus this repo's two local packs for always-testable working rules that were never converted; converted the two strongest candidates and deleted the prose they now fully cover.

- **`doc-pointer-resolves`** (`.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite`, world scope) — every rule module's `doc:` field must resolve to a real file, repo-root-relative or relative to the rule's own pack (the corpus spells it both ways, inconsistently, so the check accepts whichever interpretation resolves). Replaces the RULES.md line asking a session to "grep for and re-verify every `doc:` field by hand" after a move. Verified silent against all 49 real `doc:` fields currently in the corpus.
- **`shared-tree-immutable`** (`packs/claudinite-lifecycle`, work scope) — flags any branch commit touching `.claudinite/shared/` directly, except the update flow's own commit. Replaces the RULES.md line "Never edit anything there." Ships `blocking`, so per `consumer-safe-change` it needed either a migration record or a rehearsal-fixture discharge; since a work-scope rule is never exercised by the fixture rehearsal (which runs only `selftest` and `check_the_world`, never `check_the_work`), I discharged it with a comment in `vendoring/rehearsal/fixtures.mjs` explaining why rather than fabricating a fixture that would prove nothing — documented in the second commit.

Both checks ship with a see-it-fail fixture (a violating case and a clean case) and were verified silent against the real tree. Full suite (2674 tests), `check_the_work`, and `check_the_world` are all green.

Candidates considered but not converted this run (judgment calls or false-positive risk that didn't clear the bar — logged here rather than a separate backlog issue, since none reached the point of being built and rejected): aws-sam CORS `AllowOrigins`, chrome-extension service-worker module type and `web_accessible_resources` graph, headless-browser hardcoded browser path, macos `command -v swift` and entitlement/runtime-flag pairing, node `--test` path resolution, jwt committed key material, flutter port/plugin boundary, firebase `.gitignore`/ruleset catch-all, static-website root-relative URLs, web-speech `isFinal` trap. Several of these are strong future candidates for the next sweep.

## Changed folders

- **`.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/`** — new `worldRules/doc-pointer-resolves.mjs` check + fixture test; RULES.md loses the paragraph it now covers; VERSIONS.md row.
- **`packs/claudinite-lifecycle/`** — new `workRules/shared-tree-immutable.mjs` check + fixture test; RULES.md loses the paragraph it now covers; README.md rule/check index updated to match; `pack.mjs` version bump + VERSIONS.md row (required — this pack ships to every member).
- **`vendoring/rehearsal/fixtures.mjs`** — a documentation-only comment explaining why work-scope rules need no new fixture shape, discharging `consumer-safe-change` for the new blocking rule.

## Test plan

- [x] `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 2674 pass, 0 fail
- [x] `node engine/checks/check_the_work.mjs` — clean
- [x] `node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs` — 0 blocking
- [x] Both new checks verified silent against the real tree (not just synthetic fixtures)

Closes #1274

[{"id":5379959696,"body":"## Finding: the elimination premise does not survive contact with the files

I read every candidate site rather than working from the census summaries. **Close to none of the ~40–50 is safely eliminable.** The estimate in the issue body was derived from sweep summaries, which record *that* a pack asserts a GitHub fact but not *whether* the assertion is gratuitous. Reading them in context, almost every one is either already platform-neutral or load-bearing.

### Bucket 1 was largely a census artifact, not prose to fix

The sweeps counted the *concept* landing on Actions in practice, not GitHub vocabulary in the text. Checked line by line:

| Site | Text | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `firebase/skills/create-release-plan/SKILL.md:28,30` | "release-workflow variables", "the release workflow fails if any injected variable is unset" | already neutral |
| `macos/RULES.md:64,77` | "signing secrets being present", "in a build annotation" | already neutral |
| `spec-driven-product/RULES.md:56,127` | "gate the merge from CI", "cuts from `main`" | already neutral |
| `aws-sam/RULES.md:17` | "the last green deploy workflow" | already neutral |
| `web-scraping/RULES.md:59,154` | datacenter-IP blocks, commit-step durability | already neutral |
| `research-project/RULES.md:380` | "branch/commit/PR conventions" | cross-forge |

Genuine edits available: **1–2 marginal ones** (`firebase:50` "a workflow dispatch", `web-scraping:55` "repository secrets"), each worth one census point and each slightly *less* precise afterward. `macos/README.md:63` names GitHub Actions in a **provenance** note about a real project that genuinely used it — vaguening a factual attribution makes the doc worse, not more portable.

### Bucket 2: every candidate has a legitimate defense

- **Vendored stubs** (`chrome-extension`, `static-website` bump-version workflows) travel into member repos, where a canon reference dangles. Must stay self-contained.
- **Migration records** (`claudinite-fleet-sheepdog` ×2) are dated historical accounts. The canon says do not change historical records.
- **`task.md` files** (`claudinite-lifecycle`, `tidy-repo`, `jwt`, `product-wiki`) are read standalone by executor sessions.
- **The canary README** — the fact *is* the pack's reason to exist.
- **`claudinite-dashboard`** (`README.md:498`, `pack.mjs:37`) states the fact as the **premise** of a design decision (seed the workflow; follow the scheduler rather than `push`). It does not re-spell the withhold mechanism, and the canon rule permits A to say what it needs from B.
- **Squash-merge "restatements"** turned out not to exist: `basics` has none, and `tidy-repo/skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md:11` is a six-word parenthetical justifying its own decision rule.

### The always-loaded surface is already clean

`RULES.md` is the only text every session in every declaring repo pays for, and it is already lean: `tidy-repo/RULES.md` has **zero** GitHub mentions despite 11 credited assumptions (they live in skills and `task.mjs`, where they belong), and `basics/RULES.md`'s nine are the issue→branch→PR lifecycle itself, already delegating procedure to `git-github-advanced`.

### One genuinely ambiguous case, resolved against editing

`writing-tasks/SKILL.md:171` says `task.md` must state the **constraint** and drop the mechanism. The tracker cluster's "creation always lands an issue open and ignores a `state: closed` argument" is mechanism by that reading — but it is precisely what stops a session collapsing the two calls into one. Dropping it trades a census point for a live failure mode.

### Recommendation

**Do not run the sweep.** Landing ~40 edits to hit a number would vaguen accurate provenance, weaken standalone-readable task specs, and rewrite historical migration records — a net loss against a metric that was never a cost. The ~200 inherent assumptions are what these packs *do*; the only real lever is a forge-abstraction seam, which #959's standing decision rejects absent a second consumer.

No code changes pushed. Awaiting a decision on whether to close this as not-planned.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude

For EACH file, read it end to end and hunt for these friction signatures (this is a retrospective on how the WORK went, not what was accomplished):

1. **Misunderstandings**: a clarifying-question round-trip; the human correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent building the wrong thing and reworking it; the human restating the same request; an AskUserQuestion whose answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.
2. **Suboptimal agent actions**: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant/repeated work; re-ran a command that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing convention and had it corrected.
3. **Long wall-time waits**: independent operations run serially that could have been parallel; a padded fixed sleep that over/under-shot; a process waited out after its result was already in hand; blind long polling; re-running an already-green check. If you find one, compute real wall-clock numbers from the timestamps in the file (don't estimate).
4. **Recurring questions the human asks** that the agent should self-check proactively next time.

- which file (repo-relative-style: the `--issue-<n>--` in the filename is the GitHub issue this capture is associated with; `issue-0` means no associated issue)
- a short quote/description of the friction (what happened, what it cost)
- a concrete "what would remove this cost next time" fix — a rule, default, convention, or check
- whether it looks like a one-off/situational detail (skip) vs. a durable, reusable pattern (report)

Do NOT try to word a final pack rule or decide dedup against the existing corpus — that happens centrally afterward. Just report raw candidate findings with evidence. If a file has nothing worth reporting, say so plainly — that is a common and expected outcome, do not pad with weak findings.

Keep your final report tight: one paragraph per real finding, organized by file. If a file has nothing, one line saying so.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.

- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one — Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx or .potx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.
- skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.mjs or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one — Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. - simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
